subject: Copywriting
title: The Birth of the Ad Agency
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Birth of the Ad Agency.

hook.text: Volney Palmer opened the first ad agency in 1841. He didn't write ads—he just sold newspaper space.

buildup.text: Early agencies were middlemen. They bought space cheap from papers and sold it to advertisers for more.

discovery.text: N.W. Ayer & Son changed the model in 1869. They worked for advertisers, not papers, and wrote the copy.

twist.text: Writing ads was considered beneath serious writers. Agencies had to invent the profession of copywriter.

climax.text: By 1900, agencies like J. Walter Thompson employed artists and writers. The creative agency was born.

punchline.text: The first agencies sold space. Then they filled it.

quiz.question: What did the first advertising agencies primarily sell?

details.summary: The first advertising agencies emerged in the mid-1800s as brokers who bought newspaper space and resold it to advertisers. Over time, agencies evolved from space brokers to full-service creative shops that wrote copy, designed ads, and planned campaigns. This shift created the modern...
details.whyItMatters: The ad agency created the professional copywriter role. Understanding how agencies evolved from media brokers to creative organizations explains the tensions between art and commerce that define advertising today.
takeaways: Early agencies were media space brokers, not creative services
N.W. Ayer became the first full-service agency offering copy and design
The shift from brokering to creating established copywriting as a profession

faq.question: When did ad agencies start writing copy?
faq.answer: N.W. Ayer & Son began offering copywriting services in the 1880s, becoming the first full-service agency. Before this, advertisers wrote their own ads and agencies only handled placement. The shift created a new professional class: the advertising copywriter.

faq.question: Why did agencies evolve from space brokers to creative shops?
faq.answer: Agencies realized they could charge more and retain clients longer by creating the ads, not just placing them. Offering creative services made agencies indispensable partners rather than replaceable middlemen. This value-added model defines the agency business to this day.
